title: Will English eat Japanese?
summary: A talk, not a grammar lesson: why English words enter Japanese, and why this does not change its structure.

blocks.text: This episode is a talk about vocabulary and culture, so there is no test. The big question: will English words take over Japanese? The short answer is no, and the reasons are below.
English words enter Japanese for the same reasons they enter other languages: English is the school language, the language of technology, and it carries prestige (cool, cute, clever).
They seem more numerous than they are

Katakana makes loan words stand out on the page, especially to foreigners. Try this: open any Japanese book and count the katakana words. Most are names or invented words, not loan words. In this sentence there is just one katakana word, which is the point.

blocks.jp: 今日はコーヒーを飲みながらメールを送った。
blocks.en: Today I sent an email while drinking coffee.

blocks.text: Loan words live beside native words
Loan words usually sit next to native words instead of replacing them.

rows: the loan word has largely replaced the old one
the tiger is still 虎; the loan word is a team name

blocks.text: Foreign words arrive as **nouns**: you add する to make a verb. So they do not change how sentences are built.

blocks.en: Every morning I send my mother an email.

blocks.jp: この紙をコピーしてください。

blocks.text: Chinese words, now about sixty percent of the vocabulary, changed Japanese vocabulary but not its structure, just as French changed English vocabulary and not its structure.

items: English words enter Japanese for the same reasons they enter other languages.
Katakana makes loan words stand out, so they seem more numerous than they are.
Loan words usually live beside native words rather than replacing them.
Foreign words arrive as **nouns** (you add する to make a verb), so they do not change how sentences are built.
